common_name: Fasciata Calathea (Calathea rotundifolia 'Fasciata', Striped Round-Leaf Prayer Plant)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to deep shade; this northeastern Brazilian species is sold in the trade mainly under the older name Calathea rotundifolia 'Fasciata' and needs high humidity and fluoride-free water to look its best.

directions: Goeppertia fasciata is a wet-tropical understory species from northeastern Brazil, grown for its large, broadly rounded leaves marked with alternating bands of dark and lighter green radiating out from the midrib, the undersides a glossy deep purple. Pot in a loose, humus-rich, peat-or-coir-based mix that drains freely but never fully dries, and keep it out of direct sun, which quickly bleaches and scorches the thin leaf blades. It demands consistently high humidity and steady warmth; dry indoor air causes crisp brown leaf edges, so grouping with other prayer plants or running a humidifier nearby helps considerably. Like other Marantaceae, the leaves lift upward at night and relax flat again by morning in a visible nyctinastic rhythm.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tropical Foliage Plants
North Carolina State University Extension — NC State Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, peat-based soil in bright indirect light to part shade; 'Wavestar' is a selected form of the furry feather calathea bred for narrower, ruffled-edge foliage and benefits from the same high humidity and filtered water as the species.

directions: 'Wavestar' is a named selection of Calathea rufibarba (furry feather or velvet calathea) distinguished from the standard species by narrower, slightly undulating leaf margins that give the foliage a softly rippled look, set off by the fine velvety hairs covering both leaf surface and petiole typical of the species. The leaf undersides show the same burgundy-purple reverse that sets off the plain green upper surface. Grow it in bright, indirect light — direct sun scorches the fuzzy leaves — in a humid, draft-free spot with evenly moist, fast-draining soil, and feed lightly during the active growing season. As with other calatheas, avoid tap water where possible, since chlorine, fluoride, and mineral salts tend to cause brown leaf-tip burn over time.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — NC State Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in bright indirect light to part shade; this slow-growing Brazilian species holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit as a warm-greenhouse and houseplant subject and needs steady warmth and high humidity year-round.

directions: Ctenanthe amabilis is a compact, slow-growing understory relative of the better-known burle-marxii never-never plant, native to Brazil and introduced into cultivation in Costa Rica. Its narrow, pointed oblong leaves carry alternating zones of dark green, silvery gray, and grayish-green running parallel to the veins, and the plant may take several years to reach its modest mature height. Keep it warm (around 60–80°F), in bright but indirect light, with 60–70% humidity and evenly moist, well-drained, fertile soil — both waterlogging and prolonged dryness will stress the thin rhizomes. Like its Marantaceae relatives, the leaves rise and fold at night and relax again with morning light.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — NC State Plant Toolbox
